Video is now ubiquitous, ubiquitous enough to have its own Internet domain, ubiquitous  enough to have its own set of   research   questions about how best to use it. To address these issues, we describe a method for semi-supervised video classification, a highly  automated method for video  segmentation used in   the  context  of  online video analysis. A video is first extracted from a stream of unstructured video. Given the extracted video, we model a  set of feature vectors using a generative adversarial network (GAN). We  then train a   network  to find a  set of feature vectors that  predict the correct  label assigned to each frame within the video.  Finally,  we apply the trained model to new video streams to extract  an improved set of feature vectors for classifying a new set of unstructured video data.  Our method  is a  variant  of some methods previously developed, such as  feature engineering (Rao et al., 2010) and  video classification (Dewhurst et al., 2017). This particular  application of semi-supervised video segmentation has three  unique challenges. The first is that of finding relevant features, that is,   features that are related  to the topic of  the  video. We  introduce the  concept of features,  with the understanding that they  are related to  a topic,  but we emphasize that a  feature can be related to the  topic (and not just to the images in the original  video)  and so   can be thought of as an attribute. The second challenge relates to the  fact that the original video may be  of variable temporal length, and the generated   features will be insensitive  to timing. The third challenge is that of  learning the best features, and this is arguably the  hardest of all the challenges. A wide variety  of  different  methods have been developed to  help address these challenges. While we discuss  a range of different  approaches, we do  not claim that any one  approach is  superior. Rather, we demonstrate, in this paper, an  elegant new approach  that  has several distinct advantages over previous work. We  first present a  framework by which to  build   and evaluate GANs. Then we  introduce the notion of features  in the context of semi-supervised video segmentation, and propose  a set of simple rules for  selecting the best features for a given task.  Finally, we demonstrate that our  method can be applied to solve the  problems inherent in  video analysis.

> Automatic segmentation in CMR  images has always  been challenging  due to poor  image quality,  non-rigid motion artifacts and  complex anatomy of  heart chambers. Although deep  learning neural networks offer new hopes towards fully automated CMR  analysis, accurate segmentations still remain a problem  to learn via conventional supervision techniques since obtaining high-quality manual labels for thousands of patients remains unfeasible. The objective of our proposed method to solve this task is twofold folds; 1)  use  as less  human intervention  possible while  maintaining high performance metrics on a large dataset  (280  volunteers). And 2), achieve good results even with limited  training  samples. Since obtaining  fully labeled input  to train DL models are not feasible  in  clinical settings, we propose the novel  idea of  predicting spatial  relationships across different segments  within the model  as  self-supervisory data. While most contemporary DL-based segmentation methods heavily  rely upon well annotated inputs along multiple temporal frames during test time,  we show that predictive power can be leveraged effectively on single static image alone at run time which could serve as   fast initial reference volume  prior  to  further  multi frame processing.  We evaluated various  architecture components using  popular open datasets such as UKBB-3T, UK BB-14k and  UKBB-5T [2]. Spontaneous noise spectroscopy (SNS)   is a promising tool for measuring the hyperfine   level  coherence (HFLC) of  an atomic vapor  at microwave frequencies. In this paper, we  present a novel method for reducing the noise  in SNS measurements, resulting  in a significant improvement in  the signal-to-noise ratio. This method involves exciting the atomic vapor with a  weak  microwave  pulse,  followed by a delay period,  and then measuring the decay of the induced  polarization during the delay  period.  By  optimizing the pulse duration and delay time, we are able to achieve a noise reduction of up to  10 dB, resulting in a much clearer signal and  more accurate measurements of HFLC.  We demonstrate  this method by measuring the HFLC of a rubidium vapor at  6.8 GHz, with  a noise  reduction of 9 dB, and discuss the implications for future experiments.

Nyarlathotep,  in an effort  to avoid being assassinated by his old friend and patron god Mokuba, willed  Nyarlathotep's body to  rise forthfrom its grave with  no apparent physical or psychological wound; instead, this 'house' (of sorts) appears as a living  manifestation, fully functional  (albeit deformed), which can manifest  its intelligence by  absorbing certain psychic emanations emanating form a portion of human subconsciousness - primarily  those of the author himself. Thus Nyarlathotep takes root  where it may,  but ultimately cannot be  permanently uprooted  (to paraphrase HPL's description of his god). Wherever it goes,  however,  the 'tomb-bearer' always reappears,  and sometimes comes with  friends.

Here are some  quotes that  support  my understanding (slightly updated):

"[The  Necronomicon's] true purpose was not [only] to serve for  rituals against hostile forces  such as zombies, vampires  and their  ilk (as  one might assume it would),  but  rather  also to  serve in creating new beings - humans capable  of wielding the powers of   the Old Ones through what he dubbed the Great Scheming of Nzara. As  to  why... well, there were only too  many theories."

There you have it:  the Necronomicon's real   goal  wasn't simply defeating the dead  of humanity,  but actually getting us back together with them after  having lost them long ago.  He intended it to bring us back to  our primal roots, before  we became distracted by science  and culture that lead to  our alienation from each other and ourselves.

Also note that the first  few words contained in the book  title, "the house  of  the  serpent," reference to  ancient Greek mythology's mythological creatures.   They were the serpents with tails of  fire that  ate their own bodies until they perished from thirst. The  story seems to hint that the snake/serpent aspect (what Mokuba called his wife/daughter)  is what the  reader  meets (and has absorbed) here. So apparently the idea behind the House of  the Serpent was to create something similar  to what the serpents did in the myths, by using humans  the way they  used snakes to feed upon humans.

If  this  is true, then perhaps it would make sense  what the actual author  wanted to write about as opposed to just writing about an idea.

This academic paper introduces a novel approach for weakly supervised image segmentation using  inter extreme points geodesics. The proposed method leverages the concept of  extreme points, which are the points with maximum  and minimum   pixel values within an image,  to generate geodesic paths.  These geodesics  are computed based on a cost  function, which is  formulated using the distances between extreme points. By iteratively updating the   geodesics and  the cost function, the proposed method can  effectively  identify objects within images without relying on pixel-level annotations. The  experimental results  demonstrate that the proposed  method outperforms existing weakly supervised  segmentation methods on  various benchmark datasets, showcasing  its potential for practical applications.

Medical  image segmentation is essential  in diagnosing and predicting  various diseases. Despite  recent   advances,  most current techniques struggle  with retaining comprehensive  anatomical structures. This paper introduces SegAN, an adversarial network   using multi-scale $L_1$ loss for medical image segmentation. Experimenting with different  datasets, SegAN significantly improved the accuracy of the segmentation output while greatly preserving the anatomical structure.  Our contributions are three-fold: we adapt the adversarial  training  scheme to the image segmentation problem, replace the  commonly-used cross entropy loss with a multi-scale $L_1$  loss function, and propose  a novel  segmentation generator network. This work marks an important step toward  the clinical applications of adversarial networks in  the field of medical image  segmentation.

The   Single Chain Slip-Spring Model  is a computational method that  allows for fast rheological simulations of entangled polymers. This model utilizes graphics  processing units (GPUs) to perform these calculations, significantly increasing simulation speed compared to traditional methods.  By using this approach, researchers  can better understand and   predict the behavior of entangled  polymers  in various applications such as  polymer processing or material science. The implementation of  the slip spring model onto an NVIDIA CUDA platform demonstrates significant performance improvements over CPU based implementations  making it ideal for  large scale  entanglement dominated  flow  problems. Overall, this study provides a powerful tool for simulating complex polymeric  materials with  high accuracy  and efficiency.

This academic paper critically examines the concept of  'physical computation' and attempts to determine the  conditions  under which a physical  system can be construed as  performing computation. It provides analytical and philosophical perspectives on computation  in  diverse  physical systems,  whether natural or artificial. The paper  also debates the ontological and epistemological  problems associated with defining computation in physical systems. Based on extensive research, it formulates a set of  necessary and sufficient conditions  for physical computation, while elucidating potential counterexamples and paradoxes. It aims to delineate the  boundary between   computational and  non-computational physical systems, contributing to the understanding  of computation in theoretical computer science and physics.  Ultimately, the  paper  posits that a universal  definition of computation may not be possible,  necessitating  context-dependent definitions.

This scholarly article investigates the properties and  characteristics of Goursat  germs, which are specialized functions in  mathematical analysis. Specifically,  it  delves into the concept of  the Puisseux characteristic, which is closely related to these types of germs. By examining  various examples  and case studies,  the author aims  to provide a comprehensive understanding of this topic  within the field of mathematics and its applications in other disciplines. The findings  offer important   insights that contribute to ongoing research endeavors on singularities and smoothness concepts in differential  geometry and    algebraic  topology.  Overall, the study highlights the significance of exploring such  topics further to enrich  our knowledge base and advance future developments in relevant fields.

She and an attendant boy named Shuken would listen  at night by his room's door; it sounded as if he  sometimes fought someone off who came there, which led both  kids  to believe he might be having secret affairs with  women from  nearby towns. This paper investigates the phenomenon of  itinerant magnetism in  spin-orbit coupled Bose  gases.   We  present a theoretical study of the magnetic properties of these gases, focusing on   the  interplay between spin-orbit coupling and interactions. Our findings suggest that spin-orbit coupling can induce  itinerant magnetism in  a Bose gas,  even in the absence of an external magnetic field. We also explore the  effects of temperature and  density on the magnetic behavior of the system.  Our results provide new  insights into the magnetic properties  of spin-orbit coupled Bose gases and open  up  new avenues for experimental investigation.

DCNAS: Densely  Connected  Neural  Architecture  Search for Semantic Image Segmentation

In this paper, we present DCNAS, a novel neural  architecture search (NAS) method for semantic image segmentation. Our approach  utilizes  a densely connected network architecture that enables efficient search  and optimization of the network structure.  We propose a novel search space that includes  both the number of layers and  the  number of connections between them, allowing for a more comprehensive search of  the  network architecture.   Our method is trained using  a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning,  and we demonstrate its effectiveness on several benchmark datasets.   Our results show that DCNAS outperforms state-of-the-art NAS methods and  achieves  competitive performance with human-designed networks.

The GraphBLAS  (Graph-Based Linear Algebra System) is a software library designed to provide  efficient and flexible linear algebra operations  on graph-structured data.  While  the practical applications of GraphBLAS have been well-explored in various domains, its mathematical foundations have not been thoroughly  examined. This paper aims to fill this gap by  providing a comprehensive analysis of the mathematical underpinnings of  GraphBLAS.

We  begin   by discussing  the motivation behind GraphBLAS and how it differs from traditional linear algebra systems. We then introduce the basic  concepts and data structures used  in GraphBLAS, including graphs, matrices, and vectors. Next, we present a detailed exposition of the mathematical properties of GraphBLAS's  core operations, such as matrix-vector multiplication, sparse  matrix  representation, and  eigenvalue decomposition.

The heart of our analysis lies  in establishing the mathematical  correctness and efficiency of GraphBLAS's  algorithms. We prove that the matrix-vector multiplication operation in GraphBLAS  preserves  the linearity  and  spectral properties of the underlying graph, and that the sparse matrix representation  adopted  by  GraphBLAS leads to significant computational  savings without sacrificing accuracy.   Furthermore, we demonstrate that  the eigenvalue decomposition  algorithm in GraphBLAS is equivalent to the classic Power iteration method, while  offering improved scalability and robustness.

Our study also explores the connections between  GraphBLAS and other algebraic  frameworks, such as graph theory, linear algebra,   and machine learning. We show that GraphBLAS can be  seen   as an instance of a more general algebraic structure  known as a "graph module," which  enables  the seamless integration of   graph-based computations into existing  algebraic frameworks. Additionally, we highlight  the relevance of GraphBLAS to various  machine learning paradigms,  including deep learning and randomized algorithms.

Finally, we conclude with  a  discussion of the  implications of our  findings and future research directions. Our work  provides a solid theoretical foundation for the  continued  development and application of  GraphBLAS, paving  the  way for further advances in graph-based computing.

This paper proposes a fast end-to-end  trainable method for semi-supervised semantic segmentation of 3D medical data.  The network is  trained on  segmentations  of low-resolution   voxel datasets. The key ingredient is a voxel-to-mesh  process which converts 3D supervision from  voxels to meshes and thus enables training  on  much less data compared  to voxel segmentations. Furthermore, the resulting meshes provide additional shape-awareness. The proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised and  supervised segmentation techniques in two clinical applications.

Recent advances in  deep learning have  achieved great success in  image segmentation, especially with convolutional neural networks (CNNs). However, directly applying CNNs to large images  is computationally expensive since it  requires  processing  a huge amount of image pixels. In this paper, we present a novel framework  for natural image segmentation that integrates affinity fusion   and graph cuts. We first apply a CNN to non-overlapping patches of an input  image, and for each patch, we obtain binary labels together with uncertainties (i.e., confidence   levels of   the labels). Then, we propagate the uncertainties through an affinity fusion graph, where  the nodes represent the patches and the  edges represent similarities between the patches. By simultaneously considering  the similarities and   the uncertainties,  our framework  iteratively  refines the   segmentation based on graph cuts.   We evaluate our method on the SIFT flow dataset,  and experimental results show the advantages  of our approach compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

> Our main  results are two fast algorithms that perform boolean operations on triangular  meshes in constant amortized  memory, processing  one vertex per mesh per cycle. This allows handling complex scenes  with large numbers  (up to √n) of objects and thousands of vertices by a single processor. In practice, our algorithm  may run up to a  factor thousand times faster than existing ones. However, as expected, these efficiency gains come at the  expense  of simplicity; while previous approaches could  be described  in  just one line of pseudocode, ours need hundreds of pages.  A  notable consequence of this  increase in complexity is that unlike their simpler  predecessors,  neither our triangle rasterization nor our operation implementation can benefit  substantially from GPUs or multicore CPUs. It is possible our techniques will benefit  some applications even if   they do not fully justify their complexity by achieving  speedups beyond those achievable using  other approaches such as octree rasterization  methods. To  prove correctness  we developed several new  results about binary quadtrees, which  might generalize to quadmeshes with non-convex faces and  polygonal holes. We believe the  study of  parallel algorithms  that use similar   data structures  may yield further  interesting  insights.

The Charlier    polynomials are a set of orthogonal   polynomials   that arise  in various mathematical and physical contexts, such as quantum mechanics  and statistical physics. In this paper, we explore the relationship between Charlier polynomials  and the Hermite   functions,  which are another  important family of orthogonal  polynomials with applications in many fields. We show how Charlier polynomials can be transformed  into  Hermite  functions through a simple scaling operation,  and derive explicit formulas for the resulting polynomials. We also discuss  some interesting properties of the transformed  polynomials, including their connection to the   Gaussian distribution and their use in signal processing. Overall, our results provide new  insights into the structure and behavior of orthogonal polynomials, and have potential implications  for a wide range of scientific and engineering applications.

This  paper presents a novel approach to the max-flow  problem, a  fundamental issue  in computer vision and image  processing, particularly   in unsupervised image segmentation. The study introduces a consistent estimation method that significantly improves the  accuracy and efficiency  of  max-flow  problem solutions. The proposed  method is based on a new mathematical  model that takes into account the spatial and color information of the image, thereby enhancing the segmentation results.  The effectiveness of  the proposed method is validated through extensive experiments on various datasets, demonstrating its  superiority over existing methods in terms of both segmentation  quality and computational  efficiency. This  research opens up new  possibilities  for the development of more advanced  unsupervised image segmentation techniques.

In this paper, we explore the use of information theoretic inequalities  as bounds in superconformal field theory. Specifically, we  consider the concept  of mutual information, which measures the amount of   information that can be  extracted from one system about another. We show that mutual information can be used to bound the entropy   of a system in superconformal field  theory, providing a new way to understand   the behavior  of these systems.  We also discuss the implications of these bounds for the study  of  black holes and other extreme  objects in superconformal field theory. Overall, our work provides a  new  perspective on the   relationship between information theory  and superconformal field theory, and opens up new  avenues for research in  these areas.

The  study of  electron dynamics in crystalline semiconductors is a fundamental area of research in  condensed matter physics. This paper provides an  overview of the  current understanding   of electron  behavior in these materials, with  a focus  on the interactions between electrons and the crystal  lattice. We discuss the various theoretical models  used to describe electron  dynamics, including band structure theory, density  functional theory, and tight-binding methods. We also review experimental techniques used to probe electron behavior, such as photoelectric  spectroscopy, scanning tunneling microscopy, and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. Finally,  we highlight recent advances in the field, including the development of new materials, the  study of topological  insulators, and   the exploration of novel  electronic devices based on semiconductor  heterostructures. Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive introduction to the fascinating world of electron dynamics  in   crystalline  semiconductors.

Here  is the abstract for  the academic paper titled "Automatic Head Overcoat  Thickness Measure with NASNet-Large-Decoder Net":

Head overcoat (HOC) thickness  is an important parameter for  the  characterization of  magnetic tape media. The measurement  of HOC thickness is commonly done manually, which  is time-consuming and error-prone. In this paper,  we present an automatic HOC thickness measurement method  using a NASNet-Large-Decoder Net. Our method uses a pre-trained convolutional neural network to extract the HOC thickness from a  tape image. The network is  trained on  a large dataset of tape images  and their  corresponding HOC thickness values. The trained  network is  then  used  to predict the HOC thickness of a  given tape image. Our method is accurate, automatic, and   efficient, and it can be used as a  substitute for the conventional  manual measurement  method.

Post-mortem iris recognition is a  challenging task in biometrics  due  to the degradation and variations in the quality of the images. In recent years, deep learning techniques have shown promising results in addressing the  challenges of  iris recognition. In  this paper,  we propose a novel approach to  post-mortem iris recognition by integrating deep-learning-based image   segmentation with traditional machine learning techniques. Our approach first applies a deep learning model to segment   the iris region of interest from  the  images,   followed by  a variety of machine  learning algorithms to recognize  the iris pattern.  We evaluate our  approach on a dataset of  high-quality iris images  and  show that it outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and speed. Furthermore, we   demonstrate the generalizability of our approach by applying it to a dataset of lower quality images, which is typically  seen in  post-mortem iris recognition scenarios.

This paper presents a novel approach  to brain tumor detection  utilizing bilateral symmetry information. Leveraging  the symmetrical characteristic inherent in the human brain structure,   we introduce an  algorithm to detect asymmetrical features indicative of  potential tumors. Our method  involves   applying image  processing  techniques to MRI scans, specifically  linear and non-linear filtering, registration, and  segmentation  to extract symmetry information. This approach, compared  to other existing detection methods, potentially improves detection  rates and reduces false positives.  The proposed framework has been tested on several benchmark datasets  and has shown promising results, successfully detecting tumors with high accuracy. Our study  suggests that the integration  of symmetry information into conventional image  processing  methods can significantly  enhance the efficacy and reliability of brain tumor detection.

Abstract:

This  paper explores the concept of Snow Leopard Permutations (SLPs)   and their intriguing properties,  particularly in relation to their even and  odd threads.  SLPs  are a  novel approach  to permutations that have been shown to  have  numerous   applications in computer science    and mathematics. In this paper,  we investigate the  properties  of SLPs and their  relationships to even  and odd threads.

Our research reveals that SLPs can be divided into two distinct categories: even and odd. We demonstrate that even  SLPs  have a unique property whereby the number  of inversions in the permutation is always even, while odd SLPs have a corresponding property  whereby the number of inversions is always  odd. We  also show that  the number of even and odd SLPs  of a given length are always equal, and that they can be efficiently generated  using a  novel algorithm that  we present in this paper.

Furthermore, we explore the relationship between SLPs and other well-known concepts in combinatorics, such as Catalan numbers and Fibonacci  numbers. Our results show  that SLPs have  a close connection to these concepts and can be used to provide  new insights and perspectives on their properties.

The results of  this paper have far-reaching  implications for the field  of combinatorics and computer science. They demonstrate the versatility  and power of SLPs and their potential for application in  a wide  range of fields, from coding theory to cryptography. Our  findings  also highlight the  importance of  exploring new approaches to  permutations and combination, and the potential for innovation and discovery in this area.

In conclusion,  this paper  provides a significant contribution to  the understanding of Snow Leopard Permutations and their properties, particularly in relation  to their even and odd threads. Our  results shed new light on the field of combinatorics,  and  demonstrate the potential for  SLPs  to  be a   valuable tool in a wide range  of applications.

Our paper presents a self-supervised deep learning algorithm for robotic camera autonomou-  sly stitching images together. In contrast to prior research, which relies on the  manual cre- action of image annotations for  the visualization of surgical tools, our method generates annotations automatically.

In detail, this paper describes an approach to compositing and registering images  of robotic surgical arms autonomously, thus enabling vision-based  autonomy in robotic  surgery.

Since manual annotations for the composition  of images are tedious and  time-consuming, and because the tools move during surgery,  we  developed a self-supervision-learned  solution.

We introduce a deep- learning   architecture  for compositing  images and  use camera poses for registration.

As demonstrated  in  this  research paper, we  believe our method  outperforms methods that are in- tended for visual tracking, due to increased efficiency and  simplicity. We  compare our method with a state-of-the-art  algorithm for camera ego- pose estimation.

We present  quantitative evaluation results and show application examples. Finally,   as an important step  towards  future research,  we present an automated method for localizing surgical  tools on   the robot’s image.

Recently, the trend has been towards learning data-driven potentials for CRFs by using  features learned from a neural network. Image co-segmentation is a computer vision technique that enables two  or more images  to be segmented simultaneously, allowing for  the   detection of shared objects or regions of interest across multiple images. This technique has applications in various fields such   as object  recognition, tracking, and 3D reconstruction. With the  increasing availability of  large  image datasets, there is a growing interest in developing automatic  image co-segmentation  algorithms that can efficiently and accurately segment images without  manual intervention.

This survey provides an  overview of the  state-of-the-art techniques  in automatic image  co-segmentation, including both traditional computer  vision  methods and deep learning-based approaches.   It begins by discussing the fundamentals   of  image co-segmentation, including the different types of  co-segmentation and the challenges associated with this task. The  survey  then reviews traditional computer vision methods for co-segmentation, such as  feature-based, template-based, and graph-based approaches.

The survey also provides an in-depth analysis  of  deep learning-based methods  for image co-segmentation, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs),  recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and  generative adversarial networks (GANs).  These methods are capable of learning  complex  features and patterns from  large  datasets, and have shown  promising results in image co-segmentation  tasks.

The survey also  discusses the evaluation metrics used to measure the performance of co-segmentation algorithms, as well as  the publicly available datasets and benchmarks that can be used to evaluate these algorithms. Finally, the  survey  concludes by discussing some of the challenges and limitations of current co-segmentation methods and  identifying future research directions in   this  field.

Overall, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of  the state-of-the-art techniques in automatic image co-segmentation, and will serve as  a  useful resource for  researchers and practitioners working in this field.

This paper presents a novel gradient  vector flow (GVF)  based shape prior for optimal multi-object segmentation. The proposed GVF  shape prior overcomes the limitations of traditional shape priors by providing  a more flexible  and  effective   shape representation. The proposed GVF shape prior  is used in conjunction with a new energy  functional for optimal multi-object segmentation. This new energy  functional minimizes a combination ofRegion  competition, foreground and background color likelihoods, and the proposed GVF  shape prior. Experimental  results  show that the proposed technique outperforms  state-of-the-art methods for optimal multi-object segmentation.

This  study proposes a novel image segmentation method that combines sparse  decomposition with total variation minimization to efficiently separate  screen content images into their constituent elements. The proposed approach utilizes sparsity constraints on the representation   coefficients of each pixel, allowing for  effective separation of complex backgrounds from foreground objects  or text.  Additionally, incorporating total  variation  regularization in the objective  function ensures smooth transitions between regions while preserving  important details and edges.  Experimental results  demonstrate  superior performance  compared to existing methods, making this approach suitable for various applications  such as video surveillance analysis, visual effects  production, and  digital  signage design. Overall, our methodology offers an  efficient solution for robustly segmenting screen content images using minimal user   intervention.

In  semi-supervised learning, supervised model (sVM) learning objective typically  consist of classification in the same space of all training images, which is not the most interesting case. In this paper we  propose a novel  method to automatically learn a self-paced  contrastive feature representation  (CGPR),   which  facilitates the learning of a  variety  of  model type, which typically require the learning of the  same  input space over several epochs. A self-paced feature  representation has several advantage factors compared with standard SVM approach (cf. [1]): it  has high  dimensionality (which in turn reduces cost),  does not  introduce over-fitting in the  training data, can be used for self-paced feature learning, it is self-contained,  and  it works in most real-world applications.  Although the SVM algorithm for self-paced feature learning  has been around for some time  (see [1]), only recently it has attracted much attention in  deep learning (cf. [2]) as a way  to perform unsupervised  feature learning in  context-free deep networks.  We  also  show that  CGPR will allow  for  a new class of SVM, and for self-paced learning it solves  the issue of over-fitting. We  discuss several applications of CGPR, including medical image segmentation, which can only work when training on  fully labeled images.

We introduce a family of Nikishin  systems with periodic recurrence coefficients,  which generalize the classical periodic Nikishin system.  We study the   asymptotic behavior of these  systems  for large values of $N.$  We obtain that the  number of  states in the Markov partition of  the system  divided by $N$ converges to a well-defined   limit  as $N\rightarrow\infty.$ The  limits we obtain satisfy the so-called Weiss condition, which ensures the   convergence of the corresponding entropy  functional. We also  show that the Markov partition is asymptotically optimal. Our results show that in the  periodic  case the recurrence coefficients form an ergodic structure on the state space of the system, and we describe this structure in terms of the Weiss condition. Our proofs use a combination  of the  classical Nikishin  method and techniques from Markov  partitions.

This paper presents an active   set algorithm for estimating parameters in generalized linear models with ordered predictors. The algorithm is designed to handle situations where the  number  of predictors is  large and the predictors   are  ordered. The algorithm iteratively updates the active set of  predictors  and estimates  the parameters using  a modified Newton-Raphson method. The performance  of the algorithm is   evaluated through simulation studies and compared to other existing methods. The results show that the   proposed algorithm performs well in terms  of estimation accuracy and computational efficiency.  Overall, the active set algorithm provides a useful tool  for estimating  parameters in generalized linear models with ordered predictors.

Random Forest (RF)  classifier is widely used in many pattern recognition applications, but the method has  a few drawbacks. Firstly, the  computational complexity to calculate the splitting  criteria  based on the  whole available dataset is very high. Secondly, the usage of all the features  in the initial  random subsets makes the algorithm slow, and in some cases,  may lead to overfitting  when dealing with  large datasets. In  this paper, a Fast Random Forest (FRF) classifier is proposed to overcome these issues. The FRF classifier calculates the splitting criteria for  each tree based on  a  random subset of the dataset. Furthermore, a deep convolutional neural network  (CNN) is integrated  into the FRF classifier to map   the original  features  to higher-level features before  the   splitting criteria calculation. Simulation  results show that the  proposed FRF  classifier improves the classification accuracy.

The purpose of  this research is to develop and apply a  calibrated  surrogate  maximization method based  on linear-fractional utility functions  for  binary classification  problems. The approach aims to balance  between optimization accuracy and computational   efficiency by utilizing an adaptive calibration technique that reduces overfitting, leading to improved decision making performance. Results from extensive experiments demonstrate superior predictive power  compared with  other state-of-the-art methods while maintaining competitive computation times.  Overall, our proposed methodology  offers promising potential as an effective tool for solving real-world complex multi-class classification  tasks involving  multiple conflicting  objectives.

In  this  paper, we address the problem of medical  image segmentation  with noisy labels, which is prevalent  in real-world applications due to the expensive and tedious labeling  process. We  propose a novel approach to distilling effective supervision from a small set of labeled  images using a noisy  label  refinement strategy that leverages the intrinsic coherence and label consistency of the images. Our approach is based on the insight that, despite  the presence of noise, the labels of a small number  of carefully selected images can provide reliable and effective   supervision for training a robust segmentation model.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three public medical image  segmentation benchmarks, where we achieve  state-of-the-art performance despite  using  only  a small fraction of the available labeled  data. Our results  show that our  approach is effective  in reducing the   impact of noise and improving  the  segmentation  accuracy.

Abstract
We present MultiResUNet, a modular multimodal  biomedical image segmentation framework. It is  designed to  address the   key limitations of   state-of-the-art deep learning architectures   in  dealing with multimodal images, sizeable datasets, and utilizing transfer learning. We devise a new architecture by extensively reusing components of the popular U-Net to   enable efficient encoding of multimodal information, while keeping the model size small. We  demonstrate the  effectiveness of our approach on three  publicly available mammographic datasets for breast cancer  segmentation, showing that our  model  achieves similar  performance to U-Net while being four  times smaller. We then conduct a  thorough analysis to  demonstrate the advantages of our model over other  architectures in terms of generalization, sensitivity to multimodal information, and the ability to utilize  transfer learning. To the best  of our knowledge, our work is the first to investigate and quantify  the  impact of architectural  design on multimodal segmentation  performance and transfer learning. Code is  available at: https://github.com/ newValue/MultiResUNet.

The dielectric genome of van der  Waals heterostructures refers to the diverse  range  of materials that  can be used as  dielectric layers in these structures.  This paper provides an overview of the  dielectric properties of  various materials, including their bandgaps, dielectric constants, and thermal stability. We discuss the  impact of these  properties on the performance of van  der Waals heterostructures, such  as their optical and electronic properties.  Additionally, we  highlight the  challenges and opportunities associated with using  different  dielectric materials   in these structures,  and provide guidance for selecting the appropriate dielectric material  for a specific application. Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive overview of the dielectric genome of  van  der Waals heterostructures, and serves as a valuable resource for  researchers working in this field.

Abstract:  
Search and rescue (SAR) operations aim to locate and save individuals in dangerous  situations,  often in complex environments with large amounts  of data to process. Small target detection is a crucial step in  SAR operations to identify and locate  individuals  among complex backgrounds and cluttered environments. In this  paper, we propose a  deep learning-based  approach  for small target detection   using synthetic data generation and   distributed processing. We first generate  synthetic data sets of individuals in   various environments using specialized rendering  software.  We use convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to train small target detection models  using the synthetic data sets. The CNNs  are then   deployed on a distributed cluster to improve processing speed and accuracy. We evaluate our  proposed approach on  various real-world scenarios and achieve state-of-the-art performance compared to previous approaches. Further, our results demonstrate  the effectiveness of our method in improving search and rescue operations,  saving time and lives   in critical situations.

This paper presents a  novel approach to disease classification and segmentation using self-supervised learning and interpretability-driven sample selection. The proposed method utilizes a combination   of unsupervised and supervised learning techniques  to improve the  accuracy and interpretability of disease  classification and segmentation models. The self-supervised learning component involves training a model on unlabeled data to learn useful  representations of the  input  data, which can then be used to improve the performance of a supervised learning model. The  interpretability-driven sample selection component involves selecting a subset of the training data  that is  most  informative for improving the  interpretability of the   model. The proposed method is  applied  to the  task of classifying  and segmenting skin  lesions, and  the results  demonstrate significant improvements in accuracy and interpretability compared to  previous  methods.

The abstract for the academic  paper titled "One Network to Segment Them All:  A General, Lightweight System for Accurate 3D Medical Image Segmentation" is as follows:

This paper presents a novel deep learning-based system for accurate  3D medical image segmentation. The proposed  system utilizes  a single convolutional  neural network (CNN) to  segment multiple  organs and tissues  simultaneously, without  the  need for  separate networks for each  organ. The CNN is designed to be lightweight and  efficient, with a small   number of  parameters and a fast training time. The system is trained on a large  dataset of  3D medical images, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark tasks. The proposed approach has the potential to revolutionize  the field  of medical image segmentation,  by providing a general-purpose solution that can be  applied   to a  wide range of imaging modalities and clinical applications.

This paper presents  the  second part of  our study  on multicell coordinated beamforming with rate outage constraints. We propose efficient  approximation  algorithms to address the non-convex and NP-hard problem of minimizing the  total transmission power in a multicell  system.  The algorithms  are designed to   ensure a certain level of  signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) for each user with a specified outage probability. We introduce a two-stage approach that first solves a  relaxed problem and then refines the solution  to  meet the rate outage constraints. The proposed algorithms are shown to provide  near-optimal solutions with significantly  reduced computational complexity. Extensive simulations validate the effectiveness and efficiency  of the  proposed methods.

UNET++  is a novel deep learning architecture designed  specifically for  medical  image segmentation. It extends the original U-Net model by introducing a nested structure that allows for  more efficient and accurate processing of complex images.  The proposed architecture consists of multiple  encoder-decoder  blocks, each containing a series of  convolutional layers followed   by batch  normalization and rectified  linear unit (ReLU) activation functions.  These blocks are arranged in a hierarchical  manner, with each block building upon the output of  the previous one to create increasingly  sophisticated representations of the input image.
The key innovation of UNET++  is  its ability  to handle large and complex medical images, which  often contain   a wide range of features and structures that can be difficult to capture using traditional neural networks. By leveraging the power of convolutional neural networks (CNNs),  UNET++ is able to automatically learn and  extract these features from the input image, allowing   it to achieve state-of-the-art  performance on a  variety of  medical  imaging tasks.
Overall, UNET++ represents an important  advancement  in the field  of  medical image segmentation, providing researchers and clinicians with a powerful tool for accurately identifying and isolating specific  regions within  complex images.

This academic paper  investigates the  thermalisation process for small  random perturbations of dynamical systems. The study focuses on  understanding how these perturbations affect the long-term behavior of   the system and whether they lead to thermal  equilibrium. Through  a series of mathematical analyses and numerical simulations,  the   paper  provides  insights into the underlying mechanisms of  thermalisation and the conditions  under which it occurs. The results of  this research have implications for a wide  range of fields, including physics, engineering, and computer science, and contribute to the broader understanding of  complex systems and their behavior.

This paper proposes a novel self-learning Artificial Intelligence  (AI) framework for  advanced  segmentation and classification of skin lesions in dermoscopic images. Our unique approach revamps traditional machine learning techniques by enhancing convolutional neural  networks' capabilities, which substantially improve the diagnostic accuracy of  skin cancer. An  innovative aspect of our algorithm is its self-learning functionality,  where the AI  system  continually learns and improves its diagnostic  accuracy by updating its knowledge base with novel images   and patient data. Furthermore, the framework  is evaluated using  standard  benchmark datasets, demonstrating a superior performance compared to existing methodologies.  Therefore, this AI framework holds  significant implications for  early and accurate  skin cancer detection,  thereby  increasing the survival  rates of patients.

This paper  aims  to discuss the uncertainties associated with sunspot numbers and their  estimation,  as well as  the implications of these uncertainties on our understanding of solar activity and its impacts  on Earth's climate. The sunspot  number is a  widely used index of solar activity, but it has been subject to various sources of uncertainty throughout  its history, including  changes  in observing techniques, instrumentation, and  interpretation.

Using historical records  and modern data analysis   techniques, we estimate the uncertainties in sunspot numbers and explore their  temporal  and spatial  variations. Our results show that the uncertainties in sunspot   numbers are significant, ranging from 10% to 30%,  depending on the period  and observatory.  We  also find that  the uncertainties have changed  over time,  with larger uncertainties observed during periods of low solar activity.

The implications  of these uncertainties are far-reaching, as they affect not only  our understanding  of past solar activity but  also our ability to  predict future solar behavior and its  potential impacts on Earth's  climate. For instance, the uncertainties  in sunspot  numbers can influence the accuracy of  forecasts of space weather events,  such as coronal mass  ejections and geomagnetic storms, which  can impact satellite operations, communication systems, and power grids.

Therefore, this  study highlights the importance of  continued efforts  to improve  the accuracy and consistency of sunspot observations and to better understand the underlying  factors  contributing to the uncertainties. By doing so, we will enhance our knowledge of solar activity and its effects on Earth's  climate, enabling us to   better   anticipate and prepare for potentially disruptive space weather events.

We present a novel approach for 3D cardiovascular magnetic resonance  (MR) image segmentation based on neural  style transfer  (NST). Given a sparse manual segmentation  as the style  input, our approach transfers its morphological characteristics to an otherwise unlabeled target image. In  this work, we investigate the impact of  inconsistent manual annotations on the NST-based segmentation. We observe   that an inconsistent style input leads to  a degraded segmentation output and analyze  the reasons for this  phenomenon. To  address this problem, we  propose a simple yet effective approach  to retrieve   the true segmentation style by identifying and removing inconsistent regions in the manual style  annotation.  We demonstrate the improved  performance of our proposed method in comparison to   the state-of-the-art  on two public available  MR  datasets. Our code is  available at https://github.com/CristianRC/NST-Segmentation.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to interactive image segmentation called  LooseCut, which utilizes loosely bounded boxes to improve the  efficiency  and accuracy of  the segmentation process. Existing methods often rely  on  tightly bounding boxes that require  precise adjustments, leading to inefficiencies and user   frustration. In contrast, LooseCut  employs a new strategy that  allows users  to create loose bounds around objects, enabling faster  and more accurate segmentation.

Our approach leverages recent advances in deep learning-based segmentation techniques and incorporates a novel  optimization algorithm that refines the initial  boundaries using iterative feedback   from the user.  We evaluate LooseCut on several challenging datasets, demonstrating its   superiority over state-of-the-art methods in terms of both efficiency and accuracy. Additionally, we conduct  a user study to validate the effectiveness  and usability  of  our approach in real-world scenarios.

The key contributions   of this work  can be summarized as follows:

1. Introduction of   LooseCut, an interactive image segmentation method based on loosely bounded boxes.
2. Development of a novel optimization algorithm  that refines  initial boundaries using user feedback.
3. Demonstration of LooseCut's superiority  over existing methods  in both efficiency and accuracy  across  various datasets.
4. Validation  of the usability and effectiveness of  LooseCut through a comprehensive user study.

Overall, our proposed LooseCut method has  significant implications for improving interactive image segmentation  in  various applications such  as object recognition,  tracking, and   medical imaging analysis.

A hierarchical multilayer neural network was used to determine which pictures best  match a given search word in semantic image  segmentation. An  unsupervised approach (without testing) found that the highest  probability of  success came  when using   RNNs with multiple hidden layers over  two levels. The  two-layer multi-rate architecture has  shown strong learning performance   both  on  tasks where high-level  features were associated  at high confidence, and where these features were relatively  coarse, resulting from low resolution images. This architecture supports highly scalable  and high accuracy neural networks  capable of high level classification on diverse real-world content, yet with relatively  low memory footprint compared to convolutional or   fully convolutionsal architectures. Moreover, while only one layer  of the  neural net performed well for   training the general classifier, all of the deep  nets  learned new features by themselves. Thus it appears  that each  layer's task is  different  enough to warrant a unique type  of recurrent network architecture. Using such a different architecture should allow many types of feature learning algorithms to be introduced in future work.

> Abstract: We present  RLCorrector, an automated proofreader that corrects errors in segmentations produced by state-of-the-art connectome image analysis pipelines.   Our approach uses reinforcement learning to  learn how to fix common types of  mistakes made  during manual proofreading and then applies these corrections automatically. In experiments   on 1000 neurons  manually labeled as part of the Allen Mouse Common Coordinate  Framework (CCF) project, we show that our  method  can improve upon human  performance with respect to both accuracy and   speed.

Self-ensembling contrastive  learning is a novel approach to semi-supervised medical image segmentation that leverages multiple models trained on different  subsets of data to improve performance. The  method involves training several   models simultaneously, each  with its own set of parameters and input features, and then combining their outputs using a  self-ensembling mechanism.  This   allows the model  to learn  from both supervised and unsupervised examples,  leading to improved accuracy and robustness  in segmenting medical images.
The proposed method  was evaluated on two benchmark  datasets, including the MIMIC-III dataset and the Chest  X-ray 14 dataset,  and  compared to state-of-the-art methods. Results  showed that the  self-ensembling contrastive learning  approach outperformed  other methods by  a significant margin, achieving an average improvement of  over 5% in segmentation accuracy. Additionally, the  method demonstrated strong generalization  ability, performing   well on new, unseen  data. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of self-ensembling contrastive learning as a powerful tool for improving the accuracy and  robustness of medical image segmentation tasks.

We investigate the interference of  single and two photons in  a Mach-Zehnder interferometer  with  a nonlinear Kerr medium in one of the arms.  We find that the two-photon interference visibility is reduced by the  presence of the nonlinearity, while the single-photon  interference visibility is unaffected. This result can be explained by the  fact  that the nonlinearity breaks the symmetry between  the two arms of the  interferometer, leading to   a different phase shift for the two photons. We also find that the  two-photon  interference visibility is reduced  when the nonlinearity  is increased, while the single-photon  interference visibility  is unaffected. This result can be  explained by the fact that the nonlinearity breaks  the symmetry between the two arms   of the  interferometer, leading to a different phase shift for the two  photons.

In the digital age, the  concept of  collective memory  has evolved to encompass new forms of media and technologies that  have transformed the way we create, store, and share memories.  This paper examines the nature of collective memory in  the  digital era, exploring how   technology  has influenced our understanding and experience of  shared remembering. Through a critical  analysis of various case  studies,  including  social media platforms, online  archives, and digital museums,  this  research  investigates the ways  in which digital technologies are shaping our collective memory  and its implications for society.

The  study argues that while digital  technologies offer  unprecedented opportunities   for preserving and disseminating cultural heritage,  they  also pose  significant challenges to traditional notions of collective memory.  The paper considers issues such as data privacy,  algorithmic bias, and the ephemeral nature  of digital content, highlighting the need for a nuanced approach to understanding collective memory in the digital age.

By drawing on theories  from sociology, psychology,  and communication studies,  this paper offers a comprehensive framework for understanding collective memory in the digital era. It contributes to existing scholarship by providing fresh insights into the role of technology in  shaping our shared  memories and identities,  ultimately suggesting strategies  for fostering inclusive and diverse digital  collective memories that reflect   the complexities of human experience.

This paper  presents a novel method for automatic  head overcoat  thickness measurement based on the  application of the NASNet-Large-Decoder Net. This deep learning algorithm overcomes the limitations of traditional methods, which are mostly  manual and time-consuming. The  NASNet-Large-Decoder Net architecture utilizes a convolutional neural network  (CNN) to process input  images and accurately determine  the thickness of  the overcoat.  The algorithm was trained on a large dataset of  atomic force microscope (AFM) images and showed a high-degree  of predictive precision in   validation tests. This study's findings potentially have wide-reaching applications in the   hard disk   industry and other sectors where precise layer thickness measurements  are vital.

> "Traditional image segmentation   relies on low-level   features, such as color, texture. However,  low-level  features are sensitive to complex blurring and thus not generalizable  in  the real world. To address this challenge, we leverage semantic object recognition models to enhance the expressiveness of features  and thus improve segmentation quality. By  taking both low-level and semantic features as input,  we propose a novel Dilated Encoder Network (DE-Net) to encode   the  fused feature  to a semantic-guided encoder. To   fuse low-level and semantic features, we extend the dilated convolutions from  traditional convolutions to dilated separable convolutions, a  novel network structure.  This allows for both dense and sparse features, enabling the model  to  explore the spatial   and semantic relationships in the  image efficiently. We test the  performance of DE-Net using the Blurry Boundary Delineation (BBD) dataset.  We find that  incorporating  semantic features in a carefully designed network structure  achieves state-of-the-art performance and produces better boundary visualizations."

In  this  paper, we  propose a new approach to belief propagation  in graphical models called  Sigma  Point Belief Propagation (SPBP). Belief propagation is  an  important algorithm   in machine learning and artificial  intelligence that allows us  to  compute marginal distributions  in complex probabilistic graphical models. However,  traditional   belief propagation algorithms suffer from two   main  limitations: they  can become computationally  expensive when dealing with large graphs, and they may not be able to  capture complex dependencies  between variables.

SPBP addresses these limitations by using a  novel representation of probability distributions based on sigma points, which are  a generalization of Gaussian distributions. This allows SPBP to efficiently  represent complex distributions and perform accurate inference in large-scale graphical  models. We demonstrate  the effectiveness of SPBP  through experiments on several benchmark datasets  and compare its performance to state-of-the-art belief propagation  algorithms. Our results show that SPBP achieves better accuracy and faster convergence than existing methods  in many cases.

In addition, we analyze  the theoretical  properties of SPBP and provide bounds on its computational complexity. We also  discuss potential applications  of  SPBP in various fields such as computer vision, natural language processing, and  decision making under uncertainty.  Overall, our work presents a significant advancement in the  field of  belief propagation and  opens up new possibilities for solving challenging problems in machine learning and artificial intelligence.

The correct  positioning of tooth root is fundamental to the success of root canal treatment. However, due to the  small size and low contrast, the root   of teeth is always difficult to be segmented by  visual image analysis, especially  the fuzzy edge of tooth root, which cannot be captured by single-model segmentation method. Many segmentation algorithms have been  proposed to solve the problem, but most of them ignore the special shape characteristics of tooth root, and cannot solve the fuzzy  boundary well. This paper proposes a new segmentation method  for the  edge of  tooth root in   Cone-Beam  Computed Tomography images.   First, the landmark detection algorithm  is established  on the basis of mathematical  morphology, and the region of interest containing  tooth's root is located. Then,  the  image within the region of interest is  decomposed    adaptively under the guidance of Hoshen-Kopelman (H-K) clustering method  to  form a  multi-level image pyramid,  and the curve  of the root edge which is located farthest away from the  base  line is acquired for polynomial fitting.  On  the basis of  the root's shape features, the adaptive polynomial  fitting is carried out to achieve segmentation  of the   root edge, in which the segmentation area is expanded to include the  fuzzy region on the edge of the root. Finally, the  segmentation result is refined through the guided morphological operation  to get  the final segmented image. The effectiveness of the proposed algorithm has been validated by experimental results. Ablation experiments are  carried  out to  prove  the effectiveness of algorithm. The comparison of the proposed algorithm with  other classical   algorithms is made, and the accuracy and effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in the segmentation of root edge are verified.

Recent advances in deep learning have enabled segmenting  cell and tissue   structures in microscopy  images. However,  manual annotation of large-scale image datasets is time-consuming and costly. Furthermore,  fluorescence microscopy images  often contain missing or noisy markers, which can hinder the training  of deep learning models. In this  work, we present a method for utilizing uncertainty estimation in  deep learning segmentation of   fluorescence microscopy  images with  missing markers. Our approach  employs  a fully convolutional   network with an uncertainty module to predict segmentation masks and their associated  uncertainties.  The uncertainty module  captures the variability in the predictions by modeling the posterior distribution via a deep conditional variational network. We demonstrate the efficacy of  our approach on  a publicly available dataset  of fluorescence microscopy  images  with missing markers and achieve state-of-the-art performance.

The  paper presents an  asymptotic  expansion of a partition function related to the sinh-model. The expansion  is derived using the classical method of steepest  descent and the  resulting series  is shown   to  be in agreement with numerical calculations. This paper explores a family of random noble mean  substitutions, focusing on their properties and applications.  The noble  mean is a generalization of  the classical arithmetic,  geometric, and harmonic means. The random  noble mean substitutions introduced in  this study are defined by  a  probabilistic distribution and allow for variance in  their  values.   By analyzing the properties of these random substitutions, we demonstrate their potential applications in various areas, such as statistical analysis,  optimization algorithms, and numerical methods. Our findings reveal that these random  noble mean  substitutions offer improved flexibility  and robustness  compared  to traditional  mean substitutions. Through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, we provide insights into the  behavior and performance  of these  random noble mean  substitutions  in  different scenarios. Overall, this study contributes to the understanding of random noble mean  substitutions and their practical applications, providing a valuable framework for further research  and development in this  field.

The abstract for the academic paper titled "High-Order, Stable, And Efficient Pseudospectral Method Using Barycentric  Gegenbauer Quadratures" would  be:

We present  a stable and efficient pseudospectral scheme that achieves second-order  accuracy in approximating sparse derivative  interactions in the context of solid mechanics problems. The method  utilizes the barycentric form of the Gegenbauer quadrature  rule,  which  offers an accurate  and stable approximation  of the associated derivative kernels. By combining the barycentric quadrature with a nodal-bubble matrix format, we develop  a pseudospectral method that  is computationally efficient and  suitable for three-dimensional problems. The  proposed method is extensively evaluated on a range of numerical  examples, including static and  dynamic   analyses  of solid mechanics problems, where it  is shown to provide accurate results and demonstrate the   benefits of  high-order discretization.

The present study investigates the relationship between nonlocality and the geometric  structure of dimer algebras.  By  analyzing  various  aspects of these concepts, we aim to  provide a comprehensive understanding of their interplay in  quantum mechanics. Our results  demonstrate that  nonlocal effects are intimately connected with the central properties of dimer  algebras,  highlighting their potential implications  for  future research  on quantum systems.  Ultimately, our  findings contribute to the broader conversation regarding the nature of nonlocality and its role  in shaping the fundamental principles of quantum theory.

The  paper discusses the benefits of using state  machines in software development, including improved modularity, maintainability, and testability. It  also presents various techniques for implementing state machines  in large-scale systems, such as hierarchical state machines and statecharts. The paper concludes with  a discussion of the   challenges   and future directions in the use of state machines  for large-scale computer software and systems.

We present an  ensemble approach  to segmenting neonatal brains   on T1-weighted MR images using deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The ability to model how the intrinsic and extrinsic properties of galaxies drive their observed spectral lines is   crucial  to our understanding of galaxy evolution, the Universe  and fundamental  physics. STECKMAP is a spectral fitting software specifically designed to fit and  simultaneously model the  line and  stellar  continuum of galaxies  with complex intrinsic and extrinsic properties. STECKMAP includes models  of absorption line profiles from the latest stellar  population models (Marigo et al.  2017a), the Galactic ISM (Ivezic et al. 2019), Galactic star  formation rate (SFR) density gradients (Licquia et  al. 2015), outflows and turbulence (Baumgardt et al. 2015),  and AGN (Sulentic & Boroson 2012). In this work, we provide a thorough  overview of how   STECKMAP works, including a description of  the  input  parameters  and  a walkthrough   of the fitting  process. STECKMAP is available as an open-source extension in python with installation instructions in the documentation,   so our goal  is to provide a friendly tutorial to make the STECKMAP  experience enjoyable. Our goal  is to make galaxy fitting   with STECKMAP an approachable and user-friendly  experience.

Recent advances in  medical imaging,  such as MRI, have been instrumental in the diagnosis and treatment    of various medical conditions. However,  the sensitive nature of medical  data has prompted the  need  for secure and effective image segmentation techniques.  In  this paper,  we propose BUNET, a blind medical  image segmentation framework based  on the  Secure UNet architecture. BUNET combines the security  and  privacy of blind segmentation with the effectiveness of deep learning to provide  a robust and efficient  solution to medical  image segmentation. In our  approach, we utilize a secure artificial intelligence (AI) module that performs blind segmentation on  encrypted image data. The  module is trained  using unlabeled, encrypted image  data and a small amount of labeled, encrypted image data. During training, the  encrypted image data is processed within the secure AI module,  which prevents the exposure of the raw image data to the outside world,  including the trainer and other participants in the training process.

Our proposed method is evaluated on a public  dataset,  and we compare  its performance with that  of  a  conventional UNet. The results show that BUNET achieves a similar performance  to the UNet while providing the additional security  and privacy benefits of blind segmentation. We  believe that our proposed method can be widely used in various  medical image segmentation tasks, particularly in situations  where data privacy and security are  crucial. By combining  the strengths of deep learning  and blind  segmentation,  BUNET presents a practical and  effective solution towards secure and   private medical image segmentation.

Deep learning methods have demonstrated  tremendous advances in pixel-wise segmentation. However,  they fail  to model interaction among pixels in medical  images due  to limited data annotations. Thus, how to effectively use the  sparse annotations  is crucial   for medical segmentation.
In this paper, we  propose  a new point-based interaction approach  by employing Gaussian kernels to model interaction of all pixels   nearby the specified location (i.e., query pixel),  which can significantly boost the performance of supervised segmentation methods. This enables us to improve weakly-supervised segmentation  by using a small fraction of labeled  pixels.
Further, we introduce  the concept of sequential patch learning for the medical segmentation task. We train a deep segmentation network to perform pixel-wise  prediction  in a random manner over several adjacent  patches of the   original image, thus generating segmentation predictions for various patches of the image. We  iteratively improve the segmentation predictions by feeding them  into  an enhanced  deep  network, by taking advantage of the  sequential patch learning  paradigm. Experimental results show that our proposed work sets a new state-of-the-art weakly-supervised segmentation performance, outperforming the best known   methods by  a  significant  margin over the three  medical  datasets.
We have  also  put together the  research paper as published on arxiv.org into  a ZIP File (5.1MB) or a RAR File (3.1MB).

Recently, the coherent perfect absorption  was demonstrated in the terahertz spectrum    by using a   self-complementary metasurface made up of  one-dimensional metallic strip arrays.  However, this research  shows poor absorption and low spectral selectivity, and the absorption  band extends  from 300 Hz to 10 GHz.  Here, a broadband and energy-concentrating perfect  absorber which can  be used for  microwave imaging are designed and realized through adding a second self-complementary metasurface in the lower band region. We show  that a sharp and ultrabroadband absorption is  achieved, with a large fraction of radiation intensity accumulated in an ultrathin  layer  at the backside of the absorber. The  experimental results confirm that the designed   metasurface can produce sharp absorption at multiple  frequencies.

Recent progress in   3D medical image segmentation has primarily relied on either  convolutional neural networks (CNNs)  or transformer-based models. However, each class of  models has its drawbacks. CNNs fail to effectively  capture  global dependencies,  while transformer-based models are computationally expensive  and struggle with long-range dependencies,  which  are common in medical images. In this work,  we  propose a  new model  architecture, called CoTr, that efficiently  integrates CNNs and transformers. Our approach is  based on a hierarchical clustering procedure   that groups vertices of  a graph  in a hierarchical manner based on their similarities. We utilize this clustering   to adaptively aggregate features from CNNs  and transformers to overcome the limitations of both approaches. On the public Monkey segmentation dataset with ground truth bounding boxes, our approach achieves  92.7% mean accuracy, outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

Hierarchical image  peeling    is a novel approach to image  segmentation that utilizes scale-space filtering techniques. The proposed method  involves dividing an  image into multiple layers, each representing a different level of abstraction or  detail. Each layer is then filtered using a set of hierarchically organized filters that  are  designed to remove specific types of noise and enhance certain features in the image.
The framework  presented in this paper is flexible    and can be  applied to  a wide range of  images, including medical imagery, satellite imagery, and natural images.  It also allows for customization of the  filter sets used at each level, allowing researchers to tailor  the method to their specific needs.
Overall, hierarchical  image  peeling offers  a powerful tool for image segmentation that  combines the benefits of traditional scale-space filtering  with the flexibility of hierarchical organization.

Abstract:
In this paper, we present a one-stage approach for the instantiation  of  unknown objects from a single 2D  image to a 3D point cloud. Our  approach combines a  neural  renderer, a geometry-aware network, and  an optimization module.  Given an image of  an object with complex geometry, our neural renderer is capable of  capturing the underlying 3D structure in an  initial guess. The geometry-aware  network then  refines the initial guess  by considering the object geometry. Finally, the optimization module optimizes the refined guess to a  watertight 3D mesh. We  demonstrate the efficacy of our  approach on a benchmark of varying  complexity,  showing that  our method outperforms the  state of the art  in terms of both  quality and speed.

The proposed  research presents a novel  multilevel thresholding  algorithm that utilizes electromagnetic optimization  to enhance image processing. This approach is based on the  concept of minimizing the energy required to separate an object from  its background in  an image,  which can be achieved through the use of electromagnetic fields.
The algorithm involves dividing the image into smaller regions and applying  a series of thresholds to each region. These thresholds  are optimized using electromagnetic  fields to minimize  the amount  of  energy  required  to separate the  object from the  background. The resulting thresholds are then applied to the entire image  to   produce a binary output.
The  effectiveness of the proposed algorithm was evaluated through  simulations  and experiments with various  images. Results showed   that  the algorithm outperformed  traditional thresholding  methods in terms of accuracy and speed. Additionally, the algorithm demonstrated robustness to noise and variations  in lighting conditions.
Overall, this  study provides a new and efficient method for image thresholding that leverages the principles of electromagnetism to improve  performance and reduce computational complexity.

We consider  the design  of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that are provably fully hyperbolic.  Our construction is  based  on  a recent result in the theory of hyperbolic dynamical systems, which proves the existence of a family of structurally stable diffeomorphisms with a countable  number of  hyperbolic periodic orbits. We use this result to designdiffeomorphisms that admit a countable   number of hyperbolic equilibria, and show that these diffeomorphisms can  be used to construct  CNNs with  provably  fully hyperbolic forward dynamics. We  also show how our construction can be   used to design  CNNs with provably  fully hyperbolic  backward dynamics,  which are necessary for training fully hyperbolic CNNs using backpropagation.

We consider the problem of  detecting anomalies in   a sequence of independent observations, where the anomalies are  rare  events and the observations are drawn  from  a  known family of distributions.  We propose a sequential testing  procedure that performs optimally in the limit as the sample size goes to infinity, with  the  cost metric being the total  false  alarm rate  over  the sample interval. Our  approach  is motivated by the observation that the false alarm rate of any sequential testing procedure is proportional to  the likelihood of the observations  under the null hypothesis, and we seek to minimize this quantity by optimizing the test   procedure over all possible sequences of observations. We show that the optimal test procedure has a simple form, and we provide  a closed-form expression  for the optimal false  alarm rate. We also  show that our approach is asymptotically optimal in the sense  that  the total false alarm rate of our procedure converges to zero as the sample  size  goes to  infinity,  and we provide a bound on the convergence rate. Finally, we  demonstrate the  performance of   our procedure on a simulated data set and   compare it to existing sequential testing procedures.

In  this paper, we explore the connection between   sequential decision problems, dependent types, and generic  solutions. Sequential decision problems  are a fundamental model of decision-making under uncertainty, where an agent  must make  a sequence of decisions based on  partial information. Dependent types are a programming concept that allows type  systems to reason about the dependencies between  values. We show how dependent types can be used to encode sequential decision problems    in a way that  allows for generic solutions.

We  first introduce  a formalism for representing sequential decision problems using  dependent types. This formalism captures the structure of the problem, including the possible actions,  states, and rewards. We then demonstrate how to  use dependent types to encode a  variety  of classical decision-theoretic  concepts, such  as Markov  decision processes, partially observable Markov decision processes, and   reinforcement  learning.

Next, we develop a generic algorithm for solving  sequential decision problems encoded  with dependent types.  Our  approach  is based  on backward induction, which is a well-established method for solving  dynamic programs. However, unlike  traditional methods, our algorithm works directly with the dependent  type representation, allowing  it to handle complex problems with non-linear relationships between variables.

We evaluate  our approach through several case studies,  demonstrating its effectiveness in solving real-world decision-making problems. These include examples  from  finance,  robotics, and resource  allocation. Our results show that dependent types  provide a powerful tool for solving sequential decision problems,  and that our  generic solution can adapt to a wide range   of problem instances.

Finally,  we discuss related work and  future directions.  We compare our approach to existing methods for solving sequential decision problems, highlighting its advantages  and limitations.  We also outline potential applications of our technique  in  areas such as artificial intelligence, operations research, and programming languages. Overall, our work   provides a novel  perspective  on sequential  decision making, and  demonstrates the potential of dependent types for solving complex decision-theoretic problems.
