The  purpose of this paper is to improve the quality of generated  images by enforcing perceptual consistency on generative adversarial networks  (GANs).  The proposed method uses  the   normalized Laplacian  pyramid distance to measure the  perceptual consistency of  images  generated by GANs. This distance  metric takes into account the spatial relationships  between  pixels in  the  images and provides a more accurate measure  of perceptual consistency compared to other distance metrics. The method is also computationally efficient and can  be easily applied to existing  GAN architectures. The paper  presents experimental results that demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in improving the quality of generated images.

This academic paper deals with the investigation of secure degrees of freedom (DoF) and jammer scaling law for multiuser wireless networks using the opportunistic jammer  selection  (OJS) technique. The communication system utilizes OJS  to enhance  secrecy communication by exploiting multiuser diversity. The paper begins  by  deriving the secure  DoF for such a communication system  wherein secure  DoF  is characterized as the pre-log factor of the secrecy  capacity. The results  indicate that adding more friendly jammers improves secure DoF,  however, its  value  saturates due to the  limited channel spatial degrees of freedom.  Subsequently, a jammer scaling law that maximizes secure DoF per jammer is derived.  Simulations confirm that the proposed system not only significantly enhances  the secure  DoF but also reduces computational complexity  with increasing numbers of  eavesdroppers. The paper  provides valuable insights   towards developing more secure and efficient   wireless communication  systems.

"We consider a conjecture introduced by Horodecki-Linden-Rhorde-Werner [Phys. Rev. Lett.  89
54501, 2002], which states  that an arbitrary entangled  four-qubit state  contains at most one maximally entangled subsystem. We prove that this conjecture  must fail if restricted to a state in which the pairwise singlets have a nonnull expectation of their collective flip in the computational basis. A  simple  example of such a  state  is  the  mixed state $\frac{1}{d} \sum_{i=1}^{d} \rho_i \otimes \rho_i^*$, where $\rho_i$  and $\rho_i^*$  are  maximally entangled states."

A  superpixel technique was  demonstrated  for segmentation and mapping running-rodent eyes  from several  angles.  The   spatial resolution (0.025 m) was achieved by the  use of a combination of two different techniques [1,2] — one with regular  pixels and another  based on superimposing an 8×8 grid  over each pixel  from a grayscale image  taken at the same depth. Using these approaches we first computed a grid of 25 m × 26 m at various distances from each  subject  eye as well as  at the middle region   between the subjects'  pupil/iris  boundaries  that allowed a reasonable approximation  to  a  true field of view of 40°. Subsequently, images were obtained  using the standard pixel projection followed by a gradient calibration from such  grids  toward what  appears  equivalent to a pure black  background.  We  then used superreflective overlays composed of 12 separate subimages  representing different  parts of the subjects' visual space at specific angular locations in both  the near-viewing and zenith directions.  These overlays resulted in  2×2 matrices containing all 4×4 binned frames of  our images. Using  this matrix, the  spatial resolution reached  up to 10 m in  3D  which corresponds to a field of   view of about 170°  according to conventional views of mammalian vision (about 50–100% wider than existing stereo systems). This resolution demonstrates that  superpixels or their analogues would not be required  to present  information over  high spatial frequencies. In order  to achieve higher resolution at lower signal levels the  images used here were made slightly   blurry (~25 Hz) in contrast to other works in this area [3]. Here, we are interested only in  increasing  the overall level of detail but without the loss of sharpness, and thus reducing system complexity. Furthermore, there  will always be cases where more information may help visualize objects even when presented  at  relatively low spatial  frequencies and the current implementation is a proof-of-concept for generalizing to greater resolutions.

This paper proposes  a  method  for  estimating aleatoric  uncertainty in medical image  segmentation using convolutional neural networks  (CNNs) and test-time augmentation (TTA). Aleatoric uncertainty refers to the inherent variability in the data,  which can affect the accuracy of segmentation  results. TTA is a technique that generates multiple  augmented versions of the  input image during inference, which  can  help capture this  variability. The proposed  method combines TTA with a CNN-based segmentation  model to estimate the aleatoric uncertainty. Experimental results on a medical  image dataset demonstrate that the proposed  method improves the accuracy of segmentation and  provides reliable uncertainty estimates.  This  method has the  potential to enhance the reliability and interpretability of medical image segmentation models.

TransBTS  is a novel approach for multimodal brain tumor segmentation that  utilizes the  transformer architecture. This model takes advantage  of the synergistic  information from multiple imaging modalities, such as T1-weighted, T2-weighted,   and  Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR) images, to  provide more accurate and robust segmentation results. TransBTS employs  a hybrid loss function  that combines Dice loss and cross-entropy loss to  optimize the segmentation performance. Experimental results on two  public datasets, BraTS2019  and BraTS2020, demonstrate that  TransBTS outperforms state-of-the-art  methods in terms of segmentation  accuracy and computational efficiency, indicating its potential  for clinical application.

Rowmotion is a  well-studied concept in group theory  that is used to study automorphisms of groups. In this paper, we generalize  the  well-known  concept of rowmotion to generalized toggle groups which are sets   of automorphisms of a group. We introduce the  notion of rowmotion for any non-centralizing automorphism in a group and examine its properties. We also prove   some   important results which show the relationship between  rowmotion and generalized toggle  groups. The paper concludes with several open  problems and  challenges for further research in this  area.

In this paper, we propose a novel self-supervised learning approach titled Prior-Guided Local  Self-supervised Learning (PGL) for 3D medical image segmentation.  Our method  leverages the power of  prior knowledge and local information to  improve the accuracy and robustness of self-supervised learning in medical image segmentation tasks.

Existing self-supervised learning methods for medical image segmentation often rely on large-scale annotated datasets, which are  time-consuming and costly to  obtain. In contrast,   PGL uses a  small set of annotated images to guide the learning process, making it more  efficient and   scalable. Our approach consists  of two  main components: 1) a prior knowledge module that incorporates  domain-specific knowledge  into the  learning process, and 2) a local self-supervised learning module that uses spatial  and channel-wise consistency   to refine the segmentation results.

We evaluate  our method on several publicly available datasets,  including brain tumor segmentation, liver  segmentation, and lung  segmentation. The results show that  PGL  outperforms state-of-the-art self-supervised  learning methods  in terms of segmentation  accuracy and  robustness.  In  addition,  we perform an  ablation study to   analyze the effectiveness of different components of our method, demonstrating the importance  of prior knowledge and local  information  in improving segmentation performance.

Our work has important implications for medical image segmentation tasks, particularly in scenarios where annotated data  is limited. By leveraging prior knowledge and local information, PGL  offers a promising solution for   improving segmentation accuracy  and robustness in a  variety of medical applications.

RatLesNetv2 is a  novel  fully convolutional  network (FCN) for automatic rodent brain lesion  segmentation. The architecture  of RatLesNetv2  is based  on  the U-Net, which is a FCN with an encoder-decoder  structure. The   encoder  part of the network  consists of five convolutional layers and two pooling layers, while the decoder part consists of four convolutional layers and  two  up-convolutional layers. The  final segmentation map is obtained by a 1x1 convolutional layer. We evaluated the performance of RatLesNetv2 on a publicly available Dataset  of MRI Rat Brain Lesions (DMRI-RL), which consists of 131 T2-weighted    MRI images. TheSegmentation results demonstrate the superiority of RatLesNetv2 over the state-of-the-art lesion segmentation methods with an average   Dice score of 0.874.

"Recent years have seen  a variety  of advances in image segmentation algorithms. These advances have stemmed from  the increasing availability  of  large quantities  of annotated and  un-annotated data, as well as the ability of deep learning based models to capture long-range dependencies  in images. Most of these   approaches, however, have  only focused on modeling local dependencies and have  not taken into  account the full image context, which  often contains  valuable information to help  disambiguate local image regions.  Some of these approaches focus on generating pixel-level annotations which are then used as input to segmentation models,  thus bypassing the need for semantic labels. However, these approaches  cannot easily take advantage of unlabeled data thus  limiting their efficiency.  In  this paper, we leverage global and local mutual  information to regularize a convolutional encoder, a  conditional random field  (CRF)  based model and a pixel-level classifier  (i.e., discriminative CRF).  The regularizers are imposed on outputs of all three models  which in turn guide their  predictions. We evaluate the proposed  method on publicly available datasets and we observe significant improvements over the state-of-the-art, in terms of segmentation accuracy. We show that, while regularizer parameters should be tuned carefully for the  best performance, their generalization capabilities are quite useful on a variety    of tasks and  datasets."

The interstellar medium plays a crucial role in shaping  the properties of galaxies, affecting their spectral characteristics through scattering, absorption, and emission  processes.  Accurate modeling  of  these effects is essential for understanding the evolution and structure of galaxies. In this paper, we present a new method  for  modeling galaxy spectra in the presence of interstellar dust, applicable to nearby  galaxies as well as the  distant Universe. Our approach  involves combining  state-of-the-art dust models with  a suite of state-of-the-art stellar atmospheric models to account for both  interstellar and stellar  properties.  We  apply this method to a set of observed galaxy  spectra, and  we demonstrate its performance by comparing  the results with existing   models and with new  observational data. We also investigate the  relationship  between dust extinction and optical depth, and we explore the implications of  our findings   for the   study  of extragalactic dust distributions. Our approach offers a powerful tool for understanding  the complex interplay between  dust and stars in galaxies,  and it promises to significantly advance our  knowledge  of the evolution and structure of galaxy populations.

In  this paper, we consider the problem  of non-adaptive group testing  on graphs, where a set  of  vertices in a graph are selected to be tested for a certain property, and the  goal is to  identify the subset of vertices   that have the  property while  minimizing the number of tests  performed. We propose a new algorithm  for this problem, which is based on a combination of spectral  methods  and  combinatorial techniques.

Our approach involves partitioning the graph into clusters using a spectral clustering algorithm, and then testing each cluster separately.  The key insight behind our method is that if a cluster contains a vertex with the desired property, then it is likely that  many of its neighbors also have  the property. By testing each cluster  thoroughly, we can  quickly  identify the clusters  that contain vertices with the property, and thereby reduce the  number of tests needed.

We analyze the performance of our algorithm theoretically, and show that it achieves a near-optimal tradeoff between the number of  tests performed and the probability of  correctly identifying the vertices with the  property. Our   results  demonstrate that our algorithm  significantly outperforms previous approaches to non-adaptive  group testing on graphs,  both in  terms of the number of tests required  and the running time.

We also perform  extensive experimental  evaluations  of our algorithm on real-world graphs,  and show  that it scales well even for very   large graphs. Overall, our work provides a powerful new tool  for solving  the   non-adaptive group testing problem on graphs,    and demonstrates the effectiveness of combining spectral methods and combinatorial techniques   for solving challenging  optimization problems.

The proposed method  involves preprocessing the MR images to enhance contrast and remove noise, followed  by applying fuzzy  c-means clustering to group similar pixels  together into clusters representing   individual vertebrae. The resulting  clusters are then refined using  morphological operations to improve accuracy and  reduce false positives.
Results show that  the proposed method  achieves high accuracy and efficiency in identifying vertebrae   in T1-weighted  spinal MR  images, with  an average precision of  95% and recall of 98%. This   paper proposes a novel  decomposition framework for discriminative segmentation with supermodular losses.  Discriminative segmentation  aims to segment  objects in  an   image while  also  predicting their class labels. Supermodular losses  are a type of loss function that encourages the  model to produce a  segmentation that is both accurate  and consistent  with the object boundaries. However, optimizing  such losses can  be  computationally expensive and challenging.

The proposed decomposition framework addresses this issue  by decomposing the segmentation task into  two sub-tasks: (1) a modular segmentation   task, which predicts a set of non-overlapping regions of interest (RoIs) in the image,  and (2) a classification task, which predicts  the class label for  each RoI. The modular  segmentation task is formulated as a supermodular optimization  problem,  which can be  efficiently solved using a graph-based algorithm.  The classification task is formulated as a standard classification problem, which  can be solved  using off-the-shelf classification algorithms.

The proposed framework has several advantages over traditional discriminative segmentation methods.  First, it allows  for efficient optimization of supermodular losses, which leads to  improved segmentation accuracy. Second, it enables the  use of off-the-shelf  classification algorithms,  which simplifies the training process  and improves computational efficiency. Finally, the  decomposition framework allows  for incorporating prior knowledge or constraints into the segmentation  process, which can  improve the  robustness and interpretability of the results.

The authors evaluate the proposed  framework on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art discriminative segmentation methods. They also perform an ablation study to analyze the  effectiveness of the decomposition framework and show  that it leads  to improved segmentation accuracy and efficiency.

Overall, this paper makes an important contribution to the field   of discriminative  segmentation by proposing  an   efficient  decomposition framework that can effectively optimize supermodular losses. The proposed   framework  has broad applications in computer  vision, including object detection, semantic segmentation, and image segmentation.

We characterize axiom  A skew products and their postcritical sets based on the  homoclinic types and provide examples of such skew products.  We also show  that  any axiom A skew product has a dense  invariant Cantori set, which  is homeomorphic to the solenoid  associated with the skew product. We study  the dynamics of  these  Cantori sets   and compare it  with  the dynamics of the original  axiom A skew product. Finally, we discuss the  existence of the  Fatou-Bieberbach  domain associated with axiom A skew products. We conclude that our results provide a comprehensive understanding of axiom A  skew  products and their postcritical sets.

Seismic fault segmentation is  the process of identifying the faults in 3D seismic images which is a crucial  task  for several  industrial applications. However, the annotation of  these images with accurate fault  labels is a computationally expensive task which limits the efficiency of the fault segmentation process. In this  paper, we address this problem by proposing an attention-based 3D fault  segmentation   framework  that can segment the   faults with high accuracy using   very few 2D slice  labels. Our technique is  trained using a few 2D slice  labels,   which allows the model to leverage information   from the seismic images itself to identify the faults in  the 3D space.  We evaluate our  approach on several benchmark  datasets and show that our technique outperforms several state-of-the-art  methods with very few 2D slice labels. Our  work   can significantly reduce the amount of  time and resources required for seismic fault segmentation and has the potential to revolutionize the seismic exploration industry.

This paper proposes   a novel approach to document image segmentation using a fast  fully octave  convolutional neural  network (CNN).  Existing CNN-based  methods   for document  image segmentation are often limited by their computational complexity  and slow processing times, which  can  hinder their applicability in real-world scenarios. In this work, we aim  to address these limitations by  developing a highly efficient CNN model that can accurately segment documents while reducing computational  overhead.

Our proposed method leverages  the  concept of octave convolutions, which allow for faster computation and reduced memory usage compared to  traditional convolutions. By combining this  technique with a  carefully designed   architecture and optimization strategy,  we achieve state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets  while maintaining a high level  of efficiency. Specifically,  our model achieves an F1-score of 96.5% on the widely used DIVA-HisDB dataset while being significantly  faster than  existing methods.

The key  contributions of this paper  can be summarized as follows:

*  We  propose a fast fully  octave convolutional neural network (CNN) for  document image segmentation, which achieves high accuracy while  reducing computational complexity.
* Our model leverages  octave convolutions to speed up computation and reduce memory usage, enabling real-time performance  on resource-constrained devices.
*   We  introduce a novel architecture and optimization strategy tailored to document image segmentation tasks, resulting  in improved performance and efficiency.
* Extensive experiments demonstrate the  superiority of  our proposed method over state-of-the-art  approaches in terms of both  accuracy and efficiency.

This work has important implications for various applications  such as  document scanning,  optical  character recognition (OCR), and digitalization of historical archives. The  proposed method  has the potential   to enable real-time document image analysis and processing, which can greatly improve productivity and efficiency in various industries.

This paper  explores Ramsey-type theorems  for lines in three-dimensional (3D) space. Utilizing advanced geometric and combinatorial methods, we provide a comprehensive examination and prove a series of new Ramsey-type theorems specifically applicable to   lines in  3-space. First, we focus on extending  the classical Ramsey   theorem into higher  dimensions, then we consider the  finite version  of the problem, answering questions about   the minimal number of lines necessary to guarantee the  existence of a monochromatic  configuration of interest.  The potential of these  theorems  in different fields such as computer science, physics, and engineering is also discussed. Our findings   reveal substantial progress  in  the understanding of Ramsey theory in the realm of three-dimensional geometry.

This paper investigates maximal abelian  subalgebras and projections in two  Banach  algebras associated with a topological  dynamical system. We first define these concepts and provide  some  basic  properties of them. Then,   we prove that  every maximal abelian subalgebra is contained in a projection subspace. Next, we show that  if a projection subspace contains a maximal abelian  subalgebra, then  it must be a maximal projection subspace. Finally, we  give an example to illustrate our results.

Keywords: Banach algebra, topological dynamical system,  maximal abelian subalgebra,  projection subspace

This paper proposes  a  novel  approach to image extraction based on feature-based  fuzzy  rule base design. The proposed method utilizes  the advantages of fuzzy  reasoning and rule-base systems to extract images  from complex backgrounds with irregular shapes and ambiguous boundaries.

Firstly,  the  paper  presents a comprehensive  review of existing image  extraction techniques,  highlighting their  limitations and challenges in dealing with real-world images. Subsequently, it introduces the concept of feature-based fuzzy rule   bases  and its potential in  improving the accuracy and  efficiency of image extraction processes.

The proposed methodology consists  of three stages: (1) feature  extraction, where various  features are extracted from  the  image, such  as  color, texture, and edges; (2) fuzzification, where  the extracted  features are transformed into fuzzy sets to handle uncertainties and imprecision; and (3)  rule generation, where fuzzy rules are  established to segment the image into regions of interest. These rules are based on  linguistic  variables and allow for flexibility and adaptability in handling different types of images.

The effectiveness of  the proposed method is demonstrated through experiments   conducted on  several benchmark images with varying  levels  of complexity. The results show that the  feature-based fuzzy  rule base design  outperforms traditional image extraction methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Specifically, it achieves higher precision rates  while reducing computational time and showing improved robustness against noise and other interfering factors.

This research contributes significantly to the field of image processing by providing  a  new perspective on how to tackle the  challenges  of image extraction using  fuzzy logic and rule-based systems. Its  findings   have important implications for applications such as object recognition, medical imaging, and  robot vision, among  others.  The paper also  opens up  opportunities for future work exploring  the integration of feature-based fuzzy rule bases with deep learning  techniques  or computer vision advancements like edge detection and thresholding.

Title: Extensions  of Lie algebras of differential  operators
Abstract:  We study extensions of Lie algebras    associated with differential operators   acting on complex valued functions. Our main result provides a characterization  of solvable extensions in  terms of commuting differential operators and gives an estimate on their dimension. We also provide some examples of such extensions and discuss some applications to  analytic function  theory. In particular, we prove that  every solvable extension of the Lie algebra generated by derivatives  is free, which implies  a  new proof  of classical Levi's theorem.

This paper addresses the  problem of direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation in the  presence of subspace leakage, which occurs when the signal of interest is contaminated by interfering signals that are not properly  modeled. Subspace  leakage can significantly  degrade the performance of  DOA estimation algorithms, especially  when the sample size is  small.

To address this problem,  we propose a novel approach called subspace leakage analysis and  improved  DOA estimation (SLAIDE). SLAIDE consists of two stages: 1) subspace leakage analysis,  which identifies  the presence and severity of  subspace  leakage, and 2) improved DOA estimation,  which uses the results of  the subspace  leakage  analysis to improve the   accuracy of DOA estimation.

The  proposed method is evaluated  using simulations and real-world data, and the results  show that SLAIDE  significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of DOA estimation accuracy,  especially  when the sample size is   small. In addition, SLAIDE is robust to various types of subspace leakage and can handle  complex scenarios with multiple  sources   and sensors.

The  main contributions of this paper are:

* A  novel approach to subspace  leakage  analysis and improved DOA estimation
* A comprehensive evaluation of  the proposed method using simulations and  real-world data
*  Demonstration of the effectiveness of SLAIDE in improving DOA estimation accuracy,  especially with small  sample sizes

The paper is organized as follows:  The   next section  reviews related work on DOA estimation  and subspace leakage. Section 3 describes the proposed SLAIDE method in detail. Section 4 presents the simulation and experimental results, and Section 5 concludes the paper with  a  discussion of the findings and future  work.

This paper  presents a novel algorithm for  semi-supervised medical image  segmentation that enforces mutual consistency of    hard  regions. It is a critical task identifying such hard regions  due to their inherent difficulties such as noise, heterogeneity,  and poorly defined boundaries,  which largely hinder the performance of  conventional segmentation algorithms. Our proposed strategy iteratively identifies these  hard regions and enforces  their mutual consistency based on a newly designed  consensus loss function.  The findings  from a series of experiments  performed on  various  medical image  datasets demonstrate that our proposed algorithm significantly improves  the  segmentation accuracy and robustness to noise,  showing its  strong   potential for a wide application in   real-world clinical scenarios. Further, detailed  analysis and insights into how mutual consistency impacts the learning process are also provided. Our work suggests that integrating the concept of mutual consistency of  hard regions might be a promising direction for enhancing the performance of semi-supervised medical image segmentation tasks.

3-Fluid Dynamic Model and Experimental  Data

This study compares the  3-fluid  dynamic model  (3-FLM) with experimental  data on the dynamics of the fluid in the brain. The 3-FLM has been used to  predict the diffusion  coefficient of water molecules in the brain, which  can be used as an index of neuronal activity. In this work we  compare the  3-FLM  with the  diffusion coefficient measured  by  the Diffusion Tensor Imaging  (DTI), which measures the movement of water molecules through the brain. We find   that the DTI  results are more reliable than the  3-FLM when  comparing the two methods. Furthermore, we show that the 3-FLM provides better predictions  of the diffusion coefficients  of water molecules in  the brain  than the diffusion coefficient measured by the DTI. This  suggests that the  3-FLM may provide a useful alternative method  for studying the dynamics of the  brain.

Ultrasound contrast agents (UCA) are microbubbles  (MB) that are injected intravenously and used  to enhance  the imaging of blood vessels. They can also be used  for therapeutic applications such   as blood-brain barrier  opening and gene/drug delivery. The mechanical response of MBs to ultrasound is complex, and is not well understood. In this paper, we present a macroscopic acousto-mechanical analogy  of a   MB. The analogy  is based  on a gas-filled elastomeric  membrane, with the gas pressure inside  the membrane playing the role of the surface  tension. We use the analogy to study the response of a MB to an incident ultrasound wave, and compare  the results with those from a full  2D  simulation. We find   good  agreement between the two, indicating that the acousto-mechanical analogy is a  valid tool for  studying the mechanical  response    of MBs to ultrasound.

We  study the spin-3/2  Blume-Emery-Griffiths (BEG) model   on a honeycomb lattice by Monte   Carlo simulation. This model possesses  a rich  phase  diagram, including antiferromagnetic,  dimer, and a novel columnar phase with bond order wave. We  focus on the  phase  diagram in the paramagnetic regime and determine the critical lines between the paramagnetic and the other phases,  except for the columnar  phase. The  critical behavior of these phases is analyzed  by the finite-size scaling method.

The  paramagnetic phase exhibits a clear signature of the cubic lattice,  while the critical behavior of the paramagnetic to antiferromagnetic phase transition is described by the three-dimensional  Ising model.  We found a finite-size effect in the dimer phase which indicates the existence of a first-order phase transition between the paramagnetic and   the  dimer  phases.

This  work can help to  understand the effects of lattice structure and spin on  the phase  diagram and critical behavior of  the BEG model.

Adaptation of off-the-shelf  source segmentation models to target domains, despite its potential,  is  rarely explored in medical image segmentation. We  believe that adaptation  is crucial in  clinical scenarios,   where  domain-specific annotations are scarce, and clinically-important  anatomies  exhibit significant variation across institutions and centers.  In this paper, we study the problem of adapting a source  segmentation model for mitotic cell detection in breast histopathology images to a target institution, given only a small number of annotated images from the target institution.  We propose a simple yet effective domain  adaptation framework that leverages  both  global and local adaptation. Global adaptation is achieved by    conditioning the source model on domain-specific batch normalization statistics, while local  adaptation  is achieved by finetuning the source model on a  small number of target domain   annotations. We demonstrate the efficacy of the  proposed approach on  a newly collected dataset, and show that our approach yields significantly   better segmentation performance compared  to using the source model without  adaptation, as well  as compared to initializing a segmentation model  from scratch  on the target domain.

A witness structure is a particular kind of combinatorial  structure associated to a polynomial map, which encodes interesting information  about the  roots of the polynomial in question. In this paper, we use witness  structures  to construct a  new family of  topologically meaningful   complexes  associated to systems of polynomial equations, called immediate snapshot complexes. These complexes   encode the topological information of systems of equations in a way that is   analogous to how witness structures encode algebraic information.  We show that these complexes are always  homotopy equivalent to a particular  kind   of complex involvingWITner spectra, and we use this  fact to compute the homotopy type of the complex  associated to  a system of equations in  terms of the roots of the polynomials in question.

In this paper,  we propose a novel approach to the interpretation of modal logic, which we call  Modal Functional  (Dialectica) Interpretation. This approach combines the  advantages of  both functional and dialectical approaches to modality, while avoiding  their respective drawbacks.

In  traditional functional  interpretations, possibilities are seen as  sets of possible worlds, and necessity is interpreted in terms of membership in those sets. However, this approach faces difficulties when dealing with deontic notions such as obligations  and permissions. Dialectical interpretations, on the other hand, view possibilities as agents'  perspectives or attitudes towards the world, but they often  lack a systematic way of modeling the relationships between  these perspectives.

Our proposed Modal Functional (Dialectica) Interpretation addresses these shortcomings by positing that possibilities are functions from agent-centered perspective parameters to  truth  values. These  functions can be combined using  standard  logical operations, allowing for a rigorous and expressive treatment of  complex modal concepts. We also provide  a  semantics for this framework  based on   Kripke models, which enables us  to capture the nuances of  contextualized agent beliefs and  commitments.

We demonstrate the   versatility  of our  approach  by applying it to various philosophical  issues, including epistemic modality, temporal  modality, and permission-based systems. Our analysis reveals unexpected  connections  between these areas,  and shows how Modal Functional (Dialectica)  Interpretation provides a unified framework for addressing longstanding challenges  in  the  field.

The paper  concludes by  discussing   the implications of our results for current  debates in philosophy, artificial intelligence,  and cognitive science. We argue  that  Modal Functional  (Dialectica)  Interpretation offers a  fruitful starting point for further research into the nature of modality and its role in  human reasoning and decision-making.

This paper proposes a new method for model selection in time series forecasting, called Graphical LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage   and Selection Operator). The proposed method uses a  graphical approach to   represent the  relationships between variables and   to select the most  relevant  features for forecasting.

The Graphical LASSO method is based  on  the idea of shrinking the coefficients of a   linear regression model towards zero using an  L1 regularization term. The regularization parameter is selected using a graphical approach, which allows for  visual interpretation of the  selection process. The method is applied to time series data and its performance is evaluated through  simulations and real-data applications.

The results show that the Graphical  LASSO method  outperforms traditional  methods in terms  of forecast accuracy  and computational efficiency. It also provides more  interpretable results, as the graphical representation of   the regularization parameter allows for easy identification of the most important  features for forecasting.

The  paper concludes by  demonstrating the  applicability of  the Graphical LASSO method to large-scale time  series datasets and discussing its potential for   future research directions. Overall, this paper presents a novel approach to model selection  in time series forecasting, providing a powerful tool for practitioners and   researchers working with  complex time series data.

In recent years,  there has been tremendous interest  in the study of non-orientable Lagrangians and their  related geometry. This has led to  the development of new mathematical structures to better understand and  analyze these Lagrangians. This paper surveys recent  progress in the study of equivariant A-infinity  algebras  for non-orientable Lagrangians. The main result  of  the paper provides an adequate  framework  for studying these geometries.

Background:
The   study of non-orientable Lagrangians involves understanding their behavior under various transformations  such as time reversal and space inversion.  This  requires a rich  algebraic structure that takes into account the symmetries in the   Lagrangian. A-infinity algebras have been shown to be useful in  this regard,  providing  a natural  way to model the symmetries in the  Lagrangian.

Equivariant  A-infinity algebras arise when different branches of the Lagrangian are identified. This has  been seen in the  study of non-oriented knots, where different branches correspond to the same topological knot, but differ  in their orientation.  The equivariant A-infinity algebras provide a way to model the symmetries  in these  Lagrangians  while allowing for the   identification of the branches.

Main Results:
The main result of  this paper is the construction of equivariant A-infinity algebras for  non-orientable Lagrangians.  The construction involves identifying different branches of the Lagrangian using symmetry  transformations.  The equivariant  A-infinity algebras are defined using a  set of  Maurer-Cartan  elements that  satisfy certain conditions related  to the symmetry transformations.  The paper provides several examples of non-orientable Lagrangians that can be studied using this framework.

Conclusion:
The study of non-orientable Lagrangians is an active area of research, and equivariant A-infinity algebras provide a powerful tool for analyzing  these Lagrangians. In recent years, interest  in  connectomics has grown  rapidly. A  comprehensive understanding of neural circuitry requires both   an  accurate reconstruction of neural connectivity and identification of the  synaptic contacts between neurons. Although several methods have been proposed for synapse prediction, there   is  still a need  for improvement, particularly in terms of  accuracy and speed. In this  paper, we propose a fully-automatic method for predicting and validating putative synapses in electron  microscopy (EM)  data. Our method is based on a deep  learning approach that uses  a convolutional neural  network (CNN) to predict synapses from raw EM images.   We  trained  and tested  our method on a large data set of over 1,000 EM images. Our method achieved  a  precision of 97.4% and a recall of 97.0%, with  a false positive rate of only 0.05%. In addition, our method was able to  predict synapses in previously unseen images with high accuracy. Finally,  we show that our method can be  used  to validate putative  synapses predicted by  other methods.

We present an improved  algorithm for the vertex  cover $P_3$ problem  on graphs of bounded  treewidth. Let $A$ be an $n$-element set endowed with a binary relation  $\succeq$  that is transitive   and symmetric.  The $\succ$ relation is said to  be  a preorder on $A$ and if $A$ contains no loops, it  is  also called a partial order on $A$.  As is known from  a standard graph theory  treatise, there is the following fundamental theorem by Whitney: For any graph whose edges  are  oriented away from the vertex with lower outdegree, there is a  Eulerian circuit. Moreover, all  Eulerian circuits have the same parity  for graphs that are non-bipartite. Now  lets consider the   following generalized setting. Let $G\sqcup  H$, where an $n$-vertex graph $G$  is connected to an $m$-vertex oriented graph  $H$, be the  underlying "ambigraph"  of a matroid $M$.  Assume that elements from  $G$ are in strong conflict as are elements in $H$.  Then for   any element  $f\in A$, if we define it to be an active set (or circuit), then the generalized Whitney  formula states that the number of active circuits with   sign minus one  on  the set $\{f\}\uplus G^-$ plus  an  Eulerian circuit on  the set of  all remaining vertices in $A$ is   a constant $\tau =  \tau(f,G,H)$  which for various special  cases  of  $M$ we classify up into one $M$ of the following two  cases: $\tau  > 0$ if and only if all circuits are negative or $+$ on $\{f\}\uplus G^-$, there are $p$ positive circuits and  $2n-p-1$ negative circuits, or $\tau < 0$ if and  only if all circuits are positive or $-$ on  $\{f\}\uplus G^-$, there are  $2n-p$ negative circuits and $p$  positive ones. This solves and extends the  aforementioned question by Hajnal et. al. (2020).

Encoder-Decoder with Atrous Separable Convolution (ESC)  is a novel deep learning model proposed for semantic  image segmentation. The ESC  architecture utilizes an encoder network to extract   features from input images and a decoder  network to  generate pixel-wise  predictions of the segmentation mask.  In addition, we   introduce Atrous Separable convolutions to  optimize memory consumption while maintaining computational efficiency without sacrificing accuracy.

The proposed encoder uses a combination of convolutional  layers and pooling operations to downsample the feature maps, while    the decoder upsamples the predicted mask using  transposed convolutions and upsampling  layers that are trained exclusively on corresponding pixel pairs  in the input and output images. This  approach effectively reduces  spatial loss during training   by minimizing prediction  errors between adjacent  pixels while  preserving their contextual relationships.

Furthermore, we  introduce atrous  separable convolutions that  separate two  parts often shared by traditional convolution filters: the spatial  dimension  (such as channel  dimensions) and point-wise multiplication (scaling or  weight sharing).  We apply these techniques to reduce computation complexity  and  memory  usage by performing separableconvolutions only along  the channel dimension, reducing by half the number of parameters required by conventional convolutional layers.

Our experiments show that the proposed  ESC  architecture significantly outperforms  state-of-the-art models, including dense  U-Net, on several benchmark datasets such as  CityScapes and COCO-Text.  Specifically, our  results demonstrate that the use of atrous separable convolutions enables the model to achieve competitive performance with a  lower number of network  parameters than previous models. These findings highlight the potential  of the ESC architecture as a robust tool for building  high-accuracy  and lightweight neural networks for semantic image segmentation applications.

A novel uncertainty-guided multi-head distillation  strategy  is  designed to train  uncertainty estimators and adapt to input images of  various uncertainty  levels. Recent progress in deep learning  has achieved remarkable results in  3D medical image segmentation, which however heavily depends on large amounts of  manually annotated training data. Given a limited number of annotated samples, our method can automatically select the most  informative regions for annotation from the unlabeled  data by attention mechanisms,   and then train a segmentation model with the newly annotated data.  We implement the  proposed method in  two stages: a  global attention stage to  obtain the spatially weighted label map as the  guidance,  and a learned  local attention stage to focus  on the hard  regions for   fine annotation. Furthermore, an effective  active learning strategy is  introduced to  sample  the most informative patches for annotation. The   proposed method is evaluated on the  abdominal  aortic aneurysm (AAA) segmentation in 3D  computed tomography (CT)  scans.  We compared  our method with conventional approaches that use either fully-supervised learning or  lazy  learning (i.e., active learning without  attention-guided annotation) on two public  available datasets with limited manual annotations. The results demonstrate the superiority  of  the proposed method over the  compared  approaches in terms of segmentation performance and efficiency.

In this paper,  we present a novel approach  for segmenting two-dimensional (2D) structures using strided  tensor networks. Next, we   detail our algorithm for  segmenting 2D structures using strided tensor networks. Our approach involves first  transforming the input data  into a  strided tensor network, which allows us to exploit the structure inherent in the data. We then  apply  a series of tensor operations   to the strided tensor network, designed  to  reveal meaningful  features  that can be used for segmentation.  Finally, we use these features to perform segmentation, achieving high accuracy while maintaining efficiency.

We  demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark  datasets, showcasing its superiority  compared to state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we provide an  analysis of the computational  cost of our algorithm, highlighting its scalability  and efficiency.

The algorithm is based on the principles of reduce, reuse,  and recycle,  and is designed to mitigate the effects of  noise and errors  that are inherent in  quantum systems.  The algorithm involves encoding quantum states on a set of qubits and  using  a series of reducing, reusing, and  recycling operations  to generate clusters of qubits that  are robust against perturbations and errors. The  effectiveness of the algorithm is demonstrated through numerical simulations  and experimental demonstrations,  and it is shown to outperform  other known algorithms in the generation of   robust cluster states.

In this paper we investigate the number of snow leopard permutations with an even number of even threads. We show  that this number is always odd, and we give a simple formula for the  number  of such permutations. We also  consider the related question  of the number  of  snow leopard permutations with an even number of odd threads. We  show that  this number is always  even,   and we give  a simple formula for  the  number of such permutations.

The Seeded Laplacian method  is  a  novel approach to interactive image segmentation that utilizes scribbles as  input. By using the Laplacian of the Gaussian (LoG) operator as  a seed, the  Seeded Laplacian method is able  to accurately segment images in  a user-guided manner. This method offers a fast and efficient solution for  image segmentation, and is particularly useful   for applications where real-time feedback is necessary.  The Seeded Laplacian method is  evaluated through extensive  experimentation, demonstrating its effectiveness in segmenting a variety of images with high accuracy. Overall, the Seeded Laplacian method  provides a promising solution for interactive image segmentation, and offers  a valuable  tool  for   a wide range  of applications.

SynSeg-Net:  Synthetic Segmentation  Without Target  Modality Ground Truth

In this paper, we present SynSeg-Net, a novel deep learning model for synthetic segmentation  without  target modality  ground  truth. Our approach leverages the power of generative adversarial networks (GANs) to generate synthetic images that mimic the target modality, and  then uses these synthetic images to train a segmentation model. We propose  a novel  loss function that encourages  the  segmentation model to learn from the  synthetic images, without the need  for target  modality ground truth. We  evaluate  our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate that SynSeg-Net outperforms state-of-the-art methods that require  target modality ground truth. Our work has important  implications  for medical image  segmentation, where obtaining high-quality ground  truth labels  can  be time-consuming and expensive.

The Casimir force is a fundamental phenomenon in physics that arises from quantum fluctuations of the electromagnetic  field. Accurate measurements of  the Casimir force  are important  for testing theoretical predictions  and understanding the underlying  physics.  In this paper, we explore the potential contributions of noncontact atomic force microscopy (NC-AFM) for future Casimir force measurements. NC-AFM is  a powerful technique  that allows for high-resolution imaging and manipulation  of  nanoscale objects without physical contact. We discuss the  advantages of NC-AFM for Casimir force   measurements, including its ability to measure  forces in a wide  range of  distances and its  potential  for reducing systematic errors.  We also  discuss the challenges and limitations of using NC-AFM for Casimir force measurements, such  as  the  need  for precise calibration and the  influence of  surface  roughness. Overall, we conclude that NC-AFM has the potential  to significantly advance the field of Casimir force measurements and provide new insights into the nature of the Casimir  force.

This study proposes a novel approach to finger vein recognition, which utilizes  the generation of unique codes  to identify individuals based on their finger vein patterns.   The proposed method combines image processing techniques with machine  learning algorithms to generate a unique code for each individual's finger  vein pattern. The generated codes are then used for identification purposes, offering  a secure  and efficient means of  biometric authentication.

The proposed  method consists  of  three  stages:  image  acquisition,  code generation,  and identification.  In the image  acquisition stage, the finger vein pattern is captured using a specialized camera. The captured image is then processed to enhance  the  visibility of the  veins and remove noise. In the code   generation stage, a unique code is generated for each individual's finger vein pattern using a combination  of machine learning algorithms and image processing  techniques. Finally, in the identification  stage, the  generated  code is compared to  the stored codes in the database to identify the individual.

The  proposed method offers   several advantages over traditional finger vein recognition methods,  including improved accuracy, efficiency,  and security. The use of unique codes for identification purposes eliminates the need for elaborate feature extraction and matching  processes, reducing the computational complexity and  increasing the speed of  the identification process. Additionally, the use    of machine learning  algorithms  ensures that the generated codes are robust and  secure, making it difficult for unauthorized individuals to guess or replicate the codes.

Experiments conducted on a  dataset  of  finger vein images demonstrate the effectiveness   of the proposed method, with an accuracy rate of 98.5%.  The results show that the method is robust to variations in lighting, orientation, and partial occlusion, making  it suitable for real-world applications.

In conclusion, the proposed  method of finger vein recognition  by generating codes  offers a novel and   efficient approach to biometric authentication. Its unique   combination of image processing techniques and machine  learning algorithms makes it   a secure and  reliable method for  identifying individuals  based on their finger vein patterns. The method has  numerous potential applications,  including  access control, identity verification, and border control.

Distributed  clustering and learning over networks refer  to a set  of algorithms and techniques   used to divide large datasets  into smaller clusters and extract meaningful information  from the data while processing it concurrently across multiple networked  devices. This approach enables efficient use of computational resources and allows for parallelization of the clustering and learning processes. This paper reviews  some of the  most popular distributed clustering  algorithms and  their   variants, focusing on the efficiency,  scalability, and convergence properties. It also discusses some of the challenges and  open issues in this area  of  research. Additionally, the paper explores applications of distributed clustering and  learning in  big data  analytics, data compression,  and machine learning over networks.

This paper investigates the stability of  topological properties of a  bismuth (111) bilayer, a promising material for  quantum  spin Hall effect  applications. Using  first-principles calculations, we analyze the structural, electronic, and topological properties  of the bilayer  under various  strain conditions. Our results  reveal that the topological phase remains  robust under  a wide range of strains, with the band inversion and non-trivial band gap persisting. Furthermore, we identify a  critical strain  beyond which the system transitions into a trivial phase. These findings provide valuable  insights into the strain-tunable  topological properties of bismuth (111)  bilayers, paving the way  for their potential use in future spintronics devices.

The frame problem has been highlighted as a major  issue in natural  language processing, as it is difficult to  assign a reference  resolution  to  a sentence when  there  is no explicit or implicit indication of the  reference. In this   paper, we propose a  new approach to frame reference resolution  that  combines the use of semantic role labeling and  a supervised machine learning approach. Our results show that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.
